item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers will begin their first-ever postseason matchup with the San Diego Padres on Saturday night in what is bound to be an electric series between the two hottest teams in baseball. The Brewers, winners of 103 games during the regular season, secured the top overall seed in the postseason for the second consecutive year and are spending the week resting and preparing for what is hopefully a lengthy playoff run. The Padres, meanwhile, who tied the Brewers for the best regular season record during the month of September (18-6), hosted the Chicago Cubs in the Wild Card Series over the last two days, and swept the Brewers' rivals while outscoring them 12-1.
NL Cy Young front-runner Jacob Misiorowski will unsurprisingly start Game 1 for the Brewers on Saturday night and rookie right-hander Logan Henderson will more than likely start Game 2. Manager Pat Murphy noted that Henderson's Game 2 assignment is "subject to change," during a media session on Tuesday afternoon.
While the Brewers are known to pull tricks from their sleeves during the postseason, it's likely Murphy was referring to the possible use of a left-handed opener for Game 2 if Milwaukee ended up facing the Chicago Cubs, who had lefties Pete Crow-Armstrong and Michael Busch at the top of their lineup. Seeing as the Padres are more righty-heavy at the top of their order, with All-Stars Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado both hitting from the right side, it's more likely Henderson will serve as a traditional starter in Game 2 now that the Brewers are officially facing San Diego.
The Brewers didn't play their best baseball against San Diego this year, with a 2-4 record against the Friars to prove it, but interestingly enough, both Misiorowski and Henderson turned in strong performances against San Diego during the regular season. Let's take a closer look at the starts that Milwaukee's Game 1 and 2 starters made against their NLDS opponents during the regular season.
Both Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson tossed quality starts against the Padres during the regular season
Let's start with Misiorowski's outing against the Padres, which occurred way back on May 13. After back-to-back scoreless outings against the Washington Nationals and New York Yankees to start the month of May, Miz drew the middle contest of a three-game set against the Padres at American Family Field. Misiorowski, as he did throughout the 2026 campaign, dominated his competition, covering seven scoreless innings with 10 strikeouts while allowing just four hits.
It's important to note that the lineup Miz faced back in May looks slightly different than the one San Diego is rolling out in October, but Tatis, Machado, Jackson Merrill, Ty France, Gavin Sheets, and Xander Bogaerts all played in the May 13 contest. Tatis did collect two hits off Misiorowski, but one was an infield single on a play third baseman Luis Rengifo probably should have made, and the other was a bloop single that left the bat at 69.7 mph. The other two hits Miz allowed were also singles -- one a softly hit liner from France that Brice Turang nearly made a play on, and the other a rope to center from Sheets.
It's safe to say Misiorowski carved up the Padres when he faced them in May, but, as previously mentioned, the circumstances have changed. No offense is hotter than the Padres' right now, meaning the Brewers' flame-throwing ace will certainly be tested on Saturday night.
Henderson's start against the Padres was far more recent. The rookie right-hander was tasked with the series opener in San Diego on August 10, and therefore faced a Padres' lineup that more closely resembles the one he will see on Sunday afternoon. Henderson turned in a quality start in that mid-August outing, allowing three earned runs in 6.1 innings pitched, but did surrender two homers. One was a second-inning mistake to France -- Henderson left a changeup up in the zone and the Padres' first baseman hit a line drive homer just over the fence in left field. The other was a two-run shot from Merrill in the bottom of the seventh, when Henderson was facing the Padres' outfielder for a third time. It's important to note that Henderson most likely won't be asked to face the Padres' lineup three times on Sunday.
Even still, Henderson racked up seven strikeouts during his regular season start against the Padres, while allowing just five hits and one walk. His three earned runs tied the most he's allowed in a start, but continued his incredible streak of 23 straight starts to begin his MLB career in which he's allowed three earned runs or less. That consistency and ability to keep his team in the game is exactly what the Brewers need from Henderson in the postseason.
Ironically, despite impressive performances from their starting pitchers, the Brewers lost both Misiorowski and Henderson's starts against the Padres this year. The loss in Miz's start was due to an uncharacteristic performance from Abner Uribe in the ninth inning, whereas Henderson was handed the loss in his start after the offense couldn't rally for more than two runs. Similar starts from both Miz and Henderson this weekend would undoubtedly give the Brewers a good chance to build a 2-0 series lead before heading to San Diego for Game 3.

The best three words in sports are "Win or go home". Everything is on the line here after the Phillies rallied to win Game 2. Their season was on life support until Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hit back-to-back homers to tie the game in the 7th, and Alec Bohm hit the go-ahead homer in the 10th.
The burning question for manager Don Mattingly: Who pitches? Zack Wheeler or Aaron Nola? The answer feels obvious: go with Wheeler, the staff's ace. It would be four days between starts and three days of rest for Wheeler.
Wheeler boasts a 3.00 ERA, a 2.86 xERA, and a 3.35 FIP. He's a strikeout machine, punching out 10.72 per nine, but his walk rate has grown to 2.61 this year. He's rounding into prime form at the best time, pitching to a 1.71 ERA in five September outings.
Diving into the Phillies' pen usage, everything is on the table. The Phillies can add two extra weapons to their pen, with Aaron Nola and Jesus Luzardo as options. Andrew Painter threw 37 pitches in game two — so he might not be an option for Mattingly. The good news? Jhoan Duran will be an option since Painter saved the pen on Wednesday.
Offensively, the Phillies looked rough in the stretch entering the playoffs, but all it takes is one or two long balls to shift this game in their direction.
So far in the Wild Card round, Alec Bohm has been the guy for the Phillies, leading them with a .375 average and a 1.319 OPS. Schwarber and Harper are always a threat, but Bohm playing this well gives Philly a boost.
Braves Game 3 Lineup
- RF Ronald Acuña Jr.
- CF Michael Harris II
- SS Mauricio Dubón
- LF Mike Yastrzemski
- 3B Austin Riley
- 2B Ozzie Albies
- DH Dominic Smith
While the Phillies have multiple strong starter options for a do-or-die Game 3, the Braves have zero rotation depth, and it's showing. The options are a full bullpen game or an opener before Grant Holmes, or Grant Holmes on a short leash.
None of those are ideal options in this spot. The basic stats indicate Holmes had a solid year, posting a 3.44 ERA, but his 5.04 xERA and 4.67 FIP are terrifying in a playoff game. Holmes isn't a swing-and-miss pitcher, striking out just 6.8 hitters per nine innings, and when you can't strike hitters out, they get more chances to do damage.
Holmes also gets hit very hard, ranking in the 1st percentile in average exit velocity and third in hard-hit rate.
In this series, the Braves bats have been more reliable than the Phillies in the middle-to-bottom of the order. However, the top of the order has destroyed them. It starts with Ronald Acuna Jr. with no hits, Drake Baldwin hitting .222, and Matt Olson hitting .125.
Putting it lightly, the Braves will face an uphill battle winning this game if their three best hitters don't hit.
Sure, the Phillies totally limped into the playoffs, but the Braves have some glaring issues of their own, and they're showing up at the worst time. The lineup has been unreliable, and the rotation is a mess.
I want Wheeler or even Nola if he's starting. The Braves have no pitching answers to contain the Philadelphia big boppers.
Take the pitching and road team on the moneyline.

SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville?
It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the Cubs.
They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals.
Bowing out of the postseason after two games, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October?
They didn’t come close.
“The goal is to win, and we didn’t play well enough to do that,” third baseman Alex Bregman said. “It’s time to look in the mirror and get better.
“I know myself and a lot of these guys will be thinking about it every day of the offseason and let it fuel us. Just not good enough. We need to get better. In all areas.
“It starts now for everybody in this organization. Assess the year and come back and be better next year, because it wasn’t good enough.”
In the wake of such disappointment, there’s one overarching question: How does this not happen again?
It’s been back-to-back years of this, the Cubs dispatched by the rival Brewers in the NLDS a year ago. That was described as fuel for their fire this season, but the embers didn’t even burn long enough for a rematch.
Craig Counsell, whom the Cubs poached from those Brewers, has two early postseason exits in three seasons at the helm, with two years left on the contract that made him the game’s highest-paid skipper.
“We lost,” Counsell said. “There’s a response to it that we get to choose, and we’ve got to improve. Everybody can point at themselves and say, ‘We’ve got to get a little bit better.’
“We’re going to have to wait to accomplish the thing we really want to accomplish. … We didn’t finish it this year, and you hope that this has to be part of the journey to the ultimate prize.”
With the investments made in Counsell, Bregman, Crow-Armstrong and more, the expectations are not going to change. The Cubs will head into next season thinking World Series, just like this year.
But at least at the moment, they have a lot of questions to answer about how they’re going to get there.
What will make the 2027 group better equipped than the 2026 one?
That’s what the offseason — likely to be halted by a lengthy work stoppage — will teach us.
This was a roller-coaster campaign, with high highs and low lows, a lot of pitching injuries and a final-week downturn that came at exactly the wrong time.
The thoughts on the minds of everyone inside the losing clubhouse Wednesday were of further blows this team is about to take, the players who aren’t going to return, the pending free agents who were such a part of this group and its plan to deliver on those championship-level expectations.
“We’ll talk about the baseball plenty,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said, “but when you get through a locker room with people that you’re really close with and people that aren’t guaranteed to come back here — and not seeing this thing through the way a lot of us envisioned and believed in — that’s the stuff that doesn’t sit right and hurts.”
Perhaps most important for Jed Hoyer’s front office, the Cubs might have to replace their entire starting rotation, with lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson, plus righties Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman, all set to hit free agency.
Righties Cade Horton, Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown, plus lefty Justin Steele, make for an intriguing group of possible replacements, but all are coming off injuries, a risky play.
Then there’s the corner outfielders.
Right fielder Seiya Suzuki has been an offensive force it will be tough for the Cubs to replace; he’s expected to be one of the best hitters on the market and land a big contract.
Left fielder Ian Happ is a franchise fixture whose potential departure had teammates crying Wednesday night.
“He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said through tears.
Sentimentality is a rare reason to spend for baseball front offices. Happ didn’t have the type of offensive season he consistently has throughout his career though still played excellent defense and hit for power.
“All I can say is that I love being a Cub,” Happ said. “I’ve loved my time. I’ve loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fan base. And it’s been truly special. I don’t think there’s a better place in baseball to play.”
With decisions to make, how Hoyer crafts his roster – and how these Cubs respond to another bout of playoff disappointment – will answer that overarching question, the only question that matters:
How do the Cubs make sure this doesn’t happen again?

item.content:encoded:
After sweeping the Chicago Cubs in the NL Wild Card Series, the San Diego Padres have officially punched their ticket to the NLDS, where a matchup with the top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers awaits them. It will be the Brewers and Padres' first-ever meeting in the postseason, and there are no two hotter teams in baseball right now. The Brewers and Padres each posted a 18-6 record during the regular season portion of their September schedule, and San Diego added two more convincing wins over the Cubs this week.
While Brewers fans are relieved not to have to deal with the added stress that comes with facing the Cubs in the postseason, the Padres' recent performance undoubtedly has some fans wishing for a matchup with Craig Counsell's squad. That said, for as well as the Padres are playing right now, there are still certainly reasons for Brewers fans to be encouraged by the specific matchup. Let's take a closer look at three of the Padres' weaknesses and how they might come into play in the NLDS.
3 reasons Brewers fans should be encouraged by their NLDS matchup with the Padres
1. Question marks remain in San Diego's starting rotation
Heading into the postseason, the Padres' rotation was certainly their biggest weakness. With an elite bullpen and a surging offense, fans were unsure what San Diego would get from their starting staff in October. However, the duo of Michael King and Nick Pivetta, the latter of whom had a limited regular season workload this year due to an early-season elbow injury, dominated the Cubs in the Wild Card series, allowing just one earned run in a combined 10.1 innings. King's seven-inning shutout on Tuesday night did the heavy lifting, but Pivetta certainly impressed on Wednesday night as well.
However, even if King and Pivetta replicate their Wild Card performances in the NLDS -- likely in Games 2 and 3 -- questions remain in regard to the rest of San Diego's starting options. Trade deadline acquisitions Casey Mize, who is currently hurt, and Robbie Ray, who snuck onto the Wild Card roster but didn't pitch, haven't panned out as the Padres hoped they would. Long-time Los Angeles Dodger Walker Buehler also made the Padres' initial playoff roster, and is certainly a candidate to start a game, but his pedestrian 4.63 ERA in 32 starts this year doesn't necessarily scream "postseason starter." Not only will San Diego need King and Pivetta to repeat their incredible Wild Card performances in the NLDS, but they will also need another less obvious postseason starter to step up.
2. Padres' league-average infield defense bodes well for Brewers' offensive approach
The Cubs had an elite defensive unit in 2026, that much was obvious. In addition to Pete Crow-Armstrong's impressive performance in center field, the Cubs' infield of Alex Bregman (who was limited to DH in the Wild Card series due to a freak injury), Dansby Swanson, Nico Hoerner, and Michael Busch took away a number of would-be base hits thanks to their impressive range and sure-handedness. The Padres, while their infield unit is fine, by no means have the same elite ability to take away ground-ball base hits, and is therefore a better matchup for the Brewers' offense.
Manny Machado remains a strong defender when it comes to Outs Above Average (OAA), but his Defensive Runs Saved (DRS) total tells a different story. Ty France is a solid defensive first baseman, but the duo of Xander Bogaerts and Jake Cronenworth up the middle is below-average in the field. It's an important part of this series because the Brewers rank first in MLB in Batting Average on Balls in Play (BABIP), third in infield hits, and second in bunt hits. In other words, Milwaukee puts a lot of pressure on opposing infield defenses, and the Padres' shaky unit could come back to hurt them in this series.
3. San Diego's offense was far closer to league average for a majority of the season
The Padres' offense is on fire right now. No team posted a higher collective batting average, slugging percentage, or wRC+ than the Padres during the month of September, and only the Brewers scored more runs. Strong final months from Fernando Tatis Jr., Jackson Merrill, France, and Bogaerts led the Padres to these impressive numbers during the month of September, but for a majority of the season, San Diego's offense looked far closer to league average.
From the start of the season to the end of August, San Diego held a collective wRC+ of 98, indicating that their offensive unit was below league average for the first five months of the season. During that stretch, they ranked 20th in home runs and 22nd in runs scored. Their strong final push made their season-long numbers appear far better, but for a majority of the 2026 season, San Diego's offense was not among the best in baseball. That could matter not if the Padres' recent hot streak continues throughout October, but it's important to note this recent performance is the exception, not the norm.
2 reasons Brewers fans should be nervous about their NLDS matchup with the Padres
1. The Padres are the hottest team in baseball (aside from maybe the Brewers)
Whether their recent performance is the exception or not, there's no denying that the Padres are one of the two hottest teams in baseball, with their only threat being the team they will match up against in the NLDS. As previously mentioned, the Brewers and Padres finished first and second, respectively, in runs scored during the final month of the regular season en route to MLB-best 18-6 records. The Padres then stymied a strong Cubs' team with two comfortable wins in the NL Wild Card Series.
For the Brewers, who seemingly run into the hottest team in baseball in the early rounds of the postseason every single year, a matchup with the Padres feels like more bad luck. San Diego surged to the top Wild Card spot in the NL, secured a home postseason series, swept said series, and now carries that momentum into the NLDS. That certainly doesn't feel like a fair draw for the best team in baseball, who just completed a record-breaking 103-win regular season. Yes, the Padres have more flaws on their roster than the Brewers, but sometimes all that matters is how a team is playing when the postseason rolls around, to which the recent performance of each of these two teams would suggest fans are in for a competitive series.
2. San Diego is the only team with a better bullpen than the Brewers
The Brewers are heading into the postseason with their bullpen at its best, which is not often the case following the 162-game season. The combination of Trevor Megill, Abner Uribe, and Aaron Ashby at the back end, trade deadline acquisitions JoJo Romero and Antonio Senzatela in the middle innings, and multi-inning options like DL Hall, Chad Patrick, and Shane Drohan has Milwaukee's relief corps among the best in baseball as the playoffs arrive.
However, if there's one bullpen group that is better than the Brewers', it's the Padres' ridiculous assembly of relief weapons. Flame-throwing closer Mason Miller and his elite set-up man Adrian Morejon rightfully garner much of the attention, but other arms like Bradgley Rodriguez, Jason Adam, who just returned from the 60-day IL, and southpaw Yuki Matsui deserve respect as well. Given the strength of San Diego's bullpen and the question marks in their rotation, the pressure will be on the Brewers to build early leads and take advantage of as many scoring opportunities as possible.

What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa.
The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the postseason on Wednesday so let’s jump straight into the action!
AL Wild Card Series Game 2
Chicago White Sox 7, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago wins 2-0)
After just two games, I can’t think of any playoff participant who wants to face these White Sox. That is a sentence that no one could conceive of typing at the start of the season. Two seasons removed from suffering the most losses in MLB history and on the back of three straight losing campaigns, this upstart Chicago squad came out of nowhere to crash the postseason, starting with a two game sweep of the Astros in their own building.
They have done so by scoring early and often, the White Sox lineup a deep unit one-thru-nine with multiple ways to hurt you. They work deep counts, foul pitches off, draw walks, and can put the ball in play, but can also slug the ball out of the yard from almost any spot in the batting order. On Tuesday, they scored three unanswered runs in the first two innings to put the Astros on the back foot from the word go, and Wednesday continued the trend with the Southsiders hanging a four-spot before the home team had a chance to bat.
They had a 1-0 lead just five pitches into the game against Astros ace Hunter Brown, Sam Antonacci leading off with a double before Kyle Teel drove him home with a single. A fielding error by Nick Allen on a Miguel Vargas grounder put a pair on, and three straight singles by Andrew Benintendi, Tristan Peters, and Chase Meidroth plated three more runs with help from a Lucas Spence throwing error from center.
Credit to the Astros, they did not roll over after going down four in the first and slowly chipped into the White Sox lead. Jeremy Peña led off the bottom of the first with a booming home run that clattered off the left field wall just below the train tracks. Cam Smith hit one to almost exactly the same spot with two outs in the second. Jose Altuve narrowly snuck a solo shot into the Crawford Boxes to lead off the fourth and just like that, a 4-0 game had become a 4-3 thriller.
An inning later it looked like the Astros would pull of the improbable and complete the comeback. Smith was hit by a pitch, Peña singled, and Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases with two outs for Altuve. However, reliever Anthony Kay got Altuve to fly out to medium right field to strand all three ducks on the pond. That left the door open for the White Sox to swing the momentum back in their own favor and they did so immediately. Benintendi and Peters drew a pair of walks to open the sixth, prompting Joe Espada to call on Bryan Abreu out of the bullpen. Astros owner Jim Crane vetoed a trade of Abreu to the Twins in the final minutes of the deadline, and Abreu rewarded that faith by hanging a 3-1 slider to Meidroth, the second baseman crushing a three-run bomb to left to put the final nail in the Astros’ coffin.
After sweeping this rematch of the 2005 World Series, the White Sox advance to the ALDS where they will face the AL Central champion Guardians, first pitch of Game 1 scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday.
NL Wild Card Series Game 2
Philadelphia Phillies 4, Atlanta Braves 3
(Series tied 1-1)
The Phillies’ season was hanging by a thread until some late heroics by Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Alec Bohm sent this thrilling series to a decisive Game 3. It was a pitchers’ duel early between two starters trending in opposite directions. Tyler Mahle entered his first career playoff start with a sub-two ERA after joining the Braves from the Giants at the deadline while Cristopher Sánchez posted an ERA above five in the month of September (though will still likely wrap up his second straight runner-up finish in NL Cy Young balloting).
The one thing the two starters do have in common is first inning struggles and that certainly played out in this game. Mahle allowed a leadoff double to Trea Turner and consecutive one-out singles by Bryce Harper and Alex Bohm to allow the Phillies to jump ahead, 1-0. However, Sánchez issued a leadoff walk to Ronald Acuña Jr., who promptly stole second and scored the tying run on a Matt Olson single.
Both starters settled in from there, trading zeroes for the next five innings, until things unraveled for Sánchez and his defense in the seventh. Sean Murphy worked a leadoff walk and Ha-Seong Kim reached on a bunt single to put a pair on with no outs. Drake Baldwin then clubbed what looked like a routine liner to right, but Harper misplayed it horrifically breaking in on the ball only to watch it sail over his glove and to the wall for what was ruled as an RBI double. Sánchez intentionally walked Ozzie Albies to load the bases, and Olson made him pay with a sac fly to double the Braves lead, 3-1.
What should have been a hammer blow to the Phillies morale did not play out as such. Schwarber immediately responded with a towering leadoff shot off lefty reliever Dylan Lee, and Harper atoned for his misplay by going back-to-back to retie the game, 3-3. That sent this game to extra innings, where the much-maligned Alec Bohm continued his redemption tour. Bohm was on the bubble of being non-tendered during the offseason, but the Phillies kept him around and drove in the first run of the series with an RBI double in the first inning of Game 1. The third baseman was the ultimate hero in this one, his opposite field solo homer off rookie Didier Fuentes in the 10th to keep the Phillies season alive and force a decisive Game 3.
San Diego Padres 4, Chicago Cubs 1
(San Diego wins 2-0)
This game featured surprisingly quick hooks of both starters as neither manager wanted to risk leaving their highest leverage relievers unused. One was certainly more deserved than the other, Kevin Gausman allowing three runs on five hits in 3.1 innings. The Cubs were desperate for starting pitching at the Trade Deadline and Gausman was supposed to be their big prize. However, he flopped after making the move from the Blue Jays, pitching to a 4.83 ERA in nine starts post-deadline, and his stinker tonight was the beginning of the end of the Cubs’ season. Nick Pivetta on the other hand held Chicago to a run on three hits and two walks with four strikeouts in 3.1 innings, but Craig Stammen seemed determined to play the matchups in this one.
Ty France got things started with a double to lead off the second, advancing to third on a Jackson Merrill single, who then stole second to put a pair in scoring position for Xander Bogaerts. The veteran shortstop opened the scoring with an RBI single, which brought Ethan Salas to the plate. The 20-year-old became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a playoff game, and in his first postseason PA, he lifted a sac fly to center to plate Merrill as the Padres’ second run.
The real story of this series has been the Cubs’ inability to score. They led MLB scoring 5.25 runs per game, spearheaded by shoo-in NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and his MLB-leading 45 home runs (PCA would go 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series). They found themselves shut out through the first 12.1 innings of this series, finally breaking the seal in the fourth on a Seiya Suzuki single, Ian Happ walk, and Nico Hoerner RBI single. A Carson Kelly hit-by-pitch loaded the bases with two outs, but Dansby Swanson flew out to stand all three in place.
San Diego immediately punished them for failing to fully cash in on that scoring opportunity. Bogaerts reached on a one-out double, prompting Craig Counsell to call on Daniel Palencia in relief of Gausman. Palencia yanked a 101 mph fastball right into Sheets’ nitro zone down and in, and the lefty crushed it to right for a mammoth two-run blast.
It was all hands on deck from there from the Padres bullpen looking to protect their lead for the final five innings of the contest. They proved how terrifying a relief corps they’ve been all season, allowing just three base runners — a Michael Busch walk with two outs in the fifth, a Tyrone Taylor pinch-hit single with one out in the eighth, and a Hoerner one-out double off Mason Miller in the ninth — after the Cubs stranded the bases loaded to end the fourth.
San Diego advances to the NLDS where they will face the best team in baseball. It’s an unenviable position to come up against presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski and the 103-win Brewers. Game 1 of that series is scheduled for October 3rd with first pitch time contingent upon the result of Game 3 between Philly and Atlanta.

After a disappointing 93-loss season, Royals president of baseball operations J.J. Picollo said the team plans to be “aggressive in acquisitions.” But that aggressiveness, he cautioned, should not be confused with a willingness to spend aggressively on the payroll. He addressed the media along with manager Matt Quatraro in the team’s annual end-of-year press conference on Wednesday.
The season did not go as planned, with the team stumbling to a 12-19 start by the end of April. Picollo took addressed the slow start by saying “we’re responsible for the performance in April and May.” He did point out the World Baseball Classic kept some Royals players away from the team during spring training, making it more difficult to build team camaraderie. And injuries made it difficult for the team to climb their way out of the hole they had dug.
“We weren’t very good in April, and we weren’t very good in the beginning of May. I can’t sit here and tell you that I know we would have been good in June, July, August, and September, but if we had had those players on our roster and healthy and available, I think we could have made a better run.”
The Royals lost key players like Maikel Garcia and Vinnie Pasquantino early in the year, in addition to having their pitching staff decimated by injuries over the summer. The Royals announced changes to their medical staff, although Picollo denied the injuries were the reason for the moves. He also contended that despite all the adversity, the team has to win.
“That being said, nobody feels sorry for you. You got to go out and win.”
Here is what Picollo had to say about how he plans to address team needs this offseason.
The bullpen
”The bullpen is going to be a focus for us,” said Picollo. “There’s no question.”
Royals relievers had a 5.07 ERA, second-worst in baseball, and a league-worst 6.65 ERA in the ninth inning. The team lost closer Carlos Estévez to injury after his first game, and got disappointing performances from Lucas Erceg and Matt Strahm.
While Picollo expects the team to be aggressive, he added “I don’t want that mistaken for aggressive payroll spending.” He noted that the team was top five in spending on the bullpen over the last three years, but that spending on relievers may not be the solution due to the volatility of their performance.
“We have to look into ways at being more efficient,” he said, adding that they tried to look for that “diamond in the rough” late this year with waiver claims and small deals. They sought pitchers that presented different arm angles and pitches to give hitters varying looks.
“There’s not a clear, definitive answer on how to pull put a bullpen together. But I think the variety of ‘different looks,’ ‘different stuff’ type of relievers is the way we’re probably going to go.”
Back in August, owner John Sherman said he thought the bullpen could be “cobbled” together without spending too much money.
While Picollo highlighted the pitching of Steven Cruz and Nate Pearson down the stretch, the 2027 closer may not be on the roster right now.
“I don’t know if we’ll be able to sit here today and tell you we’ll have a closer. Internally, we don’t think we necessarily have it.”
Daniel Lynch IV, who enjoyed a breakthrough season in the bullpen, will be given a chance to compete for a starting spot next year. Lynch had a 1.96 ERA in 46 relief appearances this year, and a 6.53 ERA in 10 starts.
Starting pitching
Picollo said starting depth was their biggest priority after upgrading the bullpen. He admitted that the starting pitching depth he had amassed before the season was not nearly enough.
“It was as confident as I’ve ever been in starting pitching depth,” he said before discussing the injuries that hit the pitching staff. Cole Ragans, Kris Bubic, Ryan Bergert, and Stephen Kolek all missed significant time this season.
“So we’re never going to take starting pitching for granted.”
Next year’s rotation will feature Michael Wacha, Seth Lugo, and Noah Cameron, but the team will have to figure out who will fill the last two spots. The team expects to pick up the option of Tony Gonsolin, the former Dodgers All-Star pitcher who was signed late in the year and pitched in one game for the Royals. He could compete for a rotation spot along with Lynch, and Randy Dobnak, who impressed with a 3.51 ERA in 15 games.
Offense
As far as the offense, Picollo liked some of the underlying things they did, but ultimately the team did not score enough runs, particularly on the road. The Royals averaged 4.26 runs per game overall, finishing 21st in baseball. That was a slight improvement over their performance in 2025 when they scored 4.02 runs per game, 26th in baseball. But they finished dead last in baseball in runs on the road, averaging just 3.62 per game.
“It’s a combination of things. It’s getting on base at a greater clip. It’s running the bases well. It’s putting the ball in play when you need to with a man in scoring position. A lot is made of batting average with runners in scoring position - for us its more about ‘did you get him in?’”
He confirmed Ken Rosenthal’s report from Tuesday that hitting coach Alec Zumwalt has been reassigned to focus more on minor league development, but Picollo clarified that this was not a reflection of performance, and had been the plan all along. Zumwalt had worked with the current core of Royals hitters in the minors, and had ascended to the big league level with them. The team wants him back working with young minor league hitters, while assistant hitting coaches Marcus Thames and Connor Dawson work with the big league hitters. The Royals will likely hire another assistant hitting coach, but Picollo backed the work of Zumwalt.
“We’re not disappointed with his performance. We think he’s a very good hitting coach.”
The team will look for offensive upgrades in the outfield. Picollo noted the outfield defense regressed this season, despite the fences at Kauffman Stadium being moved in leaving less room to cover. Outfield prospect Carson Roccaforte could be in the mix, although he is left-handed and Picollo noted that the team is already very left-handed heavy.
The team will be “open to any and all ideas” on trades, even if that means trading players on the roster. Picollo added he is not interested in trading players for prospects, given their timeline and expectations to contend.
“We need to add players that help us at the major league level.”
Spending
Picollo said he does not have a specific payroll figure, but noted that ownership has approved additional spending when he has brought forward opportunities worth pursuing.
“I’ve always felt like it’s not my job to worry about the payroll. Our job is to get the most out of whatever we have,” said Picollo, noting there are teams in the playoffs with lower payrolls than the Royals, while many teams that spent a lot are sitting at home.
“I don’t think payroll is indicative of success on the field. I think success on the field comes with knowing your roster and how to get the most out of your roster and that’s our task. That’s what we need to do.”
Sherman said in August that the team is “freeing up some money” the team could invest, with about $30 million expected to come off the payroll with impending free agents.
When asked about potential long-term contracts for Jac Caglianone or Carter Jensen, Picollo deferred, saying that they typically don’t seriously consider such deals until after a player’s second year of service time. Both players just completed their first full season in the big leagues, finishing strong with each hitting over 20 home runs and posting an OPS+ over 120.
The Royals may have to work quickly to address their shortcomings simply because of the looming potential work stoppage. The collective bargaining agreement expires on December 1, which could lead to an end to free agent signings until a new labor deal is worked out.
“The aggressiveness in November is going to be important for us, as we expect the entire industry to be fairly busy.”
But it is clear the Royals have a lot do before the next season begins. The Royals entered 2026 expecting to build on back-to-back winning seasons. Instead, they finished with the fifth-worst record in baseball and now face significant questions in the bullpen, starting rotation and outfield. Picollo acknowledged that the fans demand more.
“It’s refreshing to know that our fans have high expectations. We want them to have high expectations, because we gave them reason to have high expectations,” said Picollo.
“With that comes to responsibility of getting it done. I think we feel pressure every year to win.”

Phillies' Aaron Nola Reportedly Starting vs. Braves over Zack Wheeler For MLB Playoffs Series Finale
The Philadelphia Phillies will go into Thursday's winner-take-all Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves in the National League Wild Card series with Aaron Nola starting on the mound.
Per The Athletic's Matt Gelb, Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly is going with Nola rather than using Zack Wheeler on short rest with a spot in the NLDS at stake.
As a result of their four-game losing streak last week that prevented them from clinching a playoff spot early, the Phillies had to use Wheeler on the final day of the regular season.
Wheeler allowed one run over six innings in a 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays to help Philadelphia secure its postseason berth, but the situation left his status for the wild card round unclear.
Even though Wheeler won't get the start, Mattingly told reporters after Wednesday's 4-3 win to extend the series "it'll be pretty much all hands on deck" for Game 3.
The Phillies are fortunate to have a deep starting staff that allowed them to go with All-Stars Jesús Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez in the first two games against Atlanta.
However, Game 3 left Mattingly with a decision between Nola or Wheeler. John Clark of NBC Sports Philadelphia noted Wheeler has never started a game in the regular season or playoffs on short rest.
Wheeler's only relief appearance in his MLB career was in Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS against the Arizona Diamondbacks. He tossed 1.2 scoreless innings in a 9-7 loss.
Nola will be pitching on regular rest after starting on Saturday against the Rays. He only made it through one inning, allowing three runs on four hits in a 12-1 loss.
While Nola's overall stat line this season doesn't look great with a 4.67 ERA, he did get better as the year went on. The right-hander had a 3.33 ERA in 14 starts after the All-Star break.
Nola made three starts against Atlanta this season with two coming in a five-day span from Sept. 6-11. He allowed three runs and struck out eight over 13.1 innings in those two outings last month.
The Phillies forced Game 3 against Atlanta thanks to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hitting back-to-back homers in the eighth to tie the score at three. Alec Bohm delivered the go-ahead solo homer in the top of the 10th.
Andrew Painter finished the game on the mound with three scoreless innings out of the bullpen.
Game 3 between the Phillies and Braves from Truist Park will be played at 8 p.m. ET on Thursday. The winner will advance to play the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLDS starting on Saturday.

The Philadelphia Phillies will play in Atlanta against the Braves on Thursday night with their seasons both on the line.
It’s a decisive Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series. The teams split the first two games in the best-of-three series. Only one team can move on.
Both teams entered Thursday with a bit of uncertainty about their pitching plans, but things are beginning to take shape.
According to multiple reports, the Phillies will be starting the veteran Aaron Nola on the mound. It was the most logical decision given that he’s on full rest.
It does raise the question about Zack Wheeler, though. He hasn’t pitched in this series. Would the Phillies really go out of the postseason potentially without even using him?
There’s reason to expect that Wheeler could follow Nola at some point in Thursday’s game.
Is Zack Wheeler Available?
Wheeler is available on Thursday night, according to The Athletic’s Matt Gelb.
“Nola will be on regular rest after pitching most recently in the penultimate game of the regular season Saturday, when he opened a bullpen game on two days’ rest and only threw 21 pitches,” Gelb writes. “The Phillies could also use Zack Wheeler, who is on three days’ rest, as a reliever in Game 3. Jesús Luzardo, who started Game 1 on Tuesday, is in play for an inning or two in Game 3 if needed.”
Wheeler pitched the Phillies’ regular season finale on Sunday against the Tampa Bay Rays. Philadelphia needed to win that game to ensure a playoff spot, and they did, so Wheeler’s arm was used for a good cause there.
Generally, starting pitchers then get at least four days of rest after an outing.
If Wheeler were to pitch Thursday, he would’ve gotten three days of rest — Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday.
Plenty of pitchers go on shorter rest in the playoffs, but it still comes with a risk. It throws off between-start routines and has potentially a greater injury probability.
A pitcher may also be slightly less effective if their arm isn’t feeling as fresh and rested as usual.
Wheeler, though, is one of this era’s great pitchers and had a 3.00 ERA in 28 outings in the regular season for the Phillies. He’s 36 years old now and doesn’t have a ton of time left in his career, most likely. He’d be a logical guy to trust in a big spot on Thursday night.
Of course, if the Phillies were able to win without using Wheeler, he could start Game 1 of the NLDS on Saturday. But that only matters if the Phillies get there.
Zack Wheeler Short Rest History
According to John Clark of NBC Sports Philadelphia, Wheeler has pitched in relief on short rest once in his career.
That was in Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS. The Phillies were eliminated that night, 4-2, by the Diamondbacks.
Wheeler did his part, though. He went 1.2 innings out of the pen, striking out one and walking one while not allowing a hit or a run.

Boston was already headed toward the playoffs when it surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for Rutschman. The Yankees reportedly rejected Baltimore’s asking price — then swept the Red Sox out of October.
Let’s be clear about why the Boston Red Sox acquired Adley Rutschman.
They didn’t need him to save their season.
They didn’t need him to drag them into postseason contention.
And they certainly didn’t surrender four prospects and their starting major-league catcher simply to hang a Wild Card banner.
Boston was already one of baseball’s hottest teams when it acquired Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles at the Aug. 3 trade deadline. The Red Sox had transformed their season with a remarkable summer surge and were firmly positioned to reach the postseason.
Rutschman was supposed to provide something more.
October.
The Red Sox paid an enormous price to a division rival because they believed adding a three-time All-Star catcher could help turn a playoff team into a championship team.
Instead, their postseason lasted two games.
The New York Yankees completed an embarrassing two-game sweep Wednesday night, beating Boston 9-2 after a 9-0 demolition in Game 1.
Final aggregate score: Yankees 18, Red Sox 2.
Boston managed only seven hits in 18 innings and batted .117 in the series. The Yankees did all of it without three-time American League MVP Aaron Judge, who was sidelined by a calf injury.
And Rutschman?
The expensive deadline addition Boston acquired specifically to make a difference at this time of year couldn’t make one.
Making matters considerably worse, the Yankees reportedly had their own opportunity to acquire Rutschman.
They decided Baltimore’s price was too high.
Then they sent Boston home.
Boston Didn’t Need Adley Rutschman to Reach the Playoffs
This is the most important context when evaluating the trade.
The Red Sox weren’t desperately chasing the final Wild Card position when chief baseball officer Craig Breslow made the deal.
Boston had gone 23-3 beginning July 2, establishing itself as one of baseball’s hottest teams and putting itself firmly on a postseason trajectory before Rutschman ever put on a Red Sox uniform.
That’s why simply pointing out that Boston reached the postseason after acquiring him misses the point.
Reaching October wasn’t supposed to justify the trade.
Winning in October was.
The Red Sox ultimately finished 87-75 and secured a Wild Card berth. Then the Yankees eliminated them in two games.
So what exactly did Boston’s massive deadline investment change?
Not its playoff destination and certainly not its playoff result.
Adley Rutschman Didn’t Deliver When Boston Needed Him Most
This was the stage for which Boston acquired Rutschman.
Instead, the Red Sox scored two runs in two games.
Rutschman finished the series 1-for-8 with three strikeouts and did not drive in a run as Boston’s offense was overwhelmed by Cam Schlittler and Max Fried.
And one of his most consequential moments came defensively during Boston’s disastrous sixth inning Wednesday.
With the Red Sox trailing 2-1 and desperately trying to keep their season alive, Spencer Jones reached first after swinging at a third strike from Garrett Crochet that got away from Rutschman.
Jones then stole second and advanced to third when Rutschman’s throw sailed into center field.
George Lombard Jr. followed with an RBI single.
The inning disintegrated from there.
By the time Boston finally recorded the third out, New York had scored six runs and transformed a one-run elimination game into another rout.
It would be ridiculous to blame Rutschman for Boston’s elimination. The Red Sox were comprehensively outplayed, their offense disappeared and their pitching couldn’t contain New York when the series was on the line.
But that’s precisely why the trade deserves scrutiny.
Boston didn’t surrender a collection of valuable young players for another complementary piece.
It paid for a difference-maker.
When the difference needed to be made, it wasn’t.
Look at What Boston Gave Baltimore
The price looks even more jarring now.
Baltimore received five players:
RHP Anthony Eyanson: Boston’s No. 2 prospect at the time of the trade and a top-50 prospect in baseball. He immediately became Baltimore’s top-ranked prospect.
RHP Kyson Witherspoon: Another highly regarded pitching prospect who immediately became one of the better prospects in Baltimore’s system.
OF Enddy Azocar: A promising young outfielder who added another high-upside asset to Baltimore’s farm system.
C Carlos Narváez: Boston’s starting major-league catcher, giving Baltimore an immediate replacement behind the plate.
OF Harold Rivas: The 18-year-old outfielder eventually sent to Baltimore as the player to be named later.
Boston received Rutschman, catcher Jake Rogers and cash.
Four prospects and a starting major-league catcher.
Sent directly to an American League East rival.
That’s not a routine deadline upgrade.
That’s a significant transfer of organizational value made specifically because Boston believed Rutschman could help it win immediately.
The immediate payoff?
Thirty-two regular-season games and a postseason that lasted two losses.
The Yankees Were Offered Adley Rutschman, Too. They Walked Away.
This is where Boston’s decision becomes even harder to swallow.
The Red Sox weren’t the only AL East contender that discussed Rutschman with Baltimore.
The Yankees reportedly explored acquiring him before the deadline.
According to the New York Post, Baltimore’s asking price from New York included pitching prospect Elmer Rodríguez, catcher Austin Wells, outfield prospect Yostin Pena and either Will Warren or Ryan Weathers.
The Yankees decided it was too much.
Boston decided its own massive prospect package wasn’t.
Two months later, the teams met in October.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox.
That alone doesn’t prove New York made the correct long-term decision. Prospects fail. Rutschman could return to All-Star form. The careers of the players Boston and New York retained or surrendered will ultimately determine how these decisions age.
But the immediate comparison couldn’t be much uglier for Breslow.
New York kept its catcher.
It kept its prospects.
It kept its young pitching.
And it eliminated the team that paid Baltimore’s price.
Ben Rice Made the Comparison Even More Painful
There is another piece of this that Boston probably doesn’t want to think about.
The Yankees didn’t merely decline to acquire Rutschman.
They watched one of their own young players become the kind of offensive weapon Boston hoped it was acquiring.
Ben Rice erupted for 41 home runs during the regular season.
Then he opened the postseason by destroying the Red Sox.
Rice went 4-for-5 with two home runs and six RBIs in New York’s 9-0 Game 1 victory.
Six RBIs.
Boston scored two runs in the entire series.
The Yankees didn’t need to surrender a massive package to Baltimore to find an impact bat.
They developed one.
Boston went shopping for an established star.
Then Rice helped send its expensive new catcher and the rest of the Red Sox home.
Boston Didn’t Even Get the Superstar Version of Rutschman
Boston can at least point to Rutschman’s impressive résumé.
He was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2019 MLB Draft, became the centerpiece of Baltimore’s rebuild and developed into one of baseball’s most recognizable catchers.
But the Red Sox weren’t trading for his résumé.
They were trading for what he could do in 2026 and 2027.
That’s an important distinction.
Rutschman was already on the injured list with wrist inflammation when Boston acquired him.
Once healthy, he played 32 regular-season games for the Red Sox and hit .222 with a .278 on-base percentage and .410 slugging percentage.
His OPS was .688.
He hit five home runs and drove in 13 runs.
His 92 OPS+ meant he was eight percent below league average offensively after adjusting for league and ballpark conditions.
Boston surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for an immediate upgrade and received below-average regular-season offense.
Then came October.
No transformational performance.
No postseason victory.
No series win.
Craig Breslow Made a Win-Now Trade. Boston Didn’t Win.
There is nothing inherently wrong with trading prospects.
Contending organizations sometimes become too protective of players who have never taken a major-league at-bat. Windows close. Players get hurt. Rosters change.
When an organization has an opportunity to win a championship, there are times when being aggressive is exactly the right approach.
But here’s the other side of that philosophy:
If you’re going to make a win-now trade, eventually you have to win now.
Breslow pushed a significant portion of Boston’s prospect capital into the middle of the table.
The Red Sox responded by finishing 87-75.
Then they arrived at Yankee Stadium and were outscored 18-2 in two games.
That’s not an October run.
That’s barely an October appearance.
The Yankees advanced. Boston went home before October was two days old.
And the player Breslow acquired as his blockbuster deadline upgrade produced neither the offensive impact nor the postseason difference Boston was paying for.
Meanwhile, Baltimore Gets to Keep All Five Players
This is the part that could hurt Boston considerably longer than Wednesday night’s loss.
Baltimore doesn’t need all four prospects to become stars for this trade to sting the Red Sox.
It doesn’t even need two of them to become stars.
If Eyanson develops into a quality major-league starter, or Witherspoon reaches his upside, or Azocar or Rivas eventually develops into an everyday player, Boston could spend years watching a division rival benefit from its deadline gamble.
Narváez is already a major-league catcher.
The Orioles essentially converted one player approaching his final season of club control into five assets.
Boston acquired the short-term star.
Baltimore acquired years of potential value.
And the Orioles didn’t have to wait long to see the first part of their gamble work.
Rutschman’s first postseason with Boston lasted two games.
Now Boston May Have to Pay for Rutschman Again
That’s what makes this more than simply a failed 2026 deadline gamble.
Rutschman can become a free agent after the 2027 season.
Boston therefore has another major decision coming.
The Red Sox can attempt to sign him to a lucrative extension, committing significant long-term money to a catcher whose offensive production has declined from his early-career peak and who has dealt with injuries.
They can let him play out 2027 and risk watching him depart as a free agent roughly 17 months after surrendering four prospects and Narváez to acquire him.
Or they can eventually trade him and attempt to recover some of the organizational value they sent Baltimore.
None looks particularly attractive this morning.
And Boston should be especially careful about allowing the enormous acquisition cost to influence its next decision.
The prospects are gone regardless.
Paying Rutschman a huge extension because Boston already paid dearly to acquire him would be classic sunk-cost thinking.
The next decision has to be based on what Rutschman is likely to provide going forward, not what Boston surrendered to get him.
He could make this entire discussion look foolish next season. Rutschman is talented enough to rebound, produce another All-Star season and become an important part of a championship contender.
But that’s a 2027 argument.
We know what happened in 2026.
Boston was already headed toward the postseason.
Baltimore put an enormous price on Rutschman.
The Yankees looked at that price and walked away.
The Red Sox paid it.
Then those two teams met in October.
New York outscored Boston 18-2, swept the Red Sox in two games and advanced without Aaron Judge.
Boston went home.
And Baltimore still has all five players.

In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023.
“Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a little bit, it's the same as we did [after Game 1]: Turn the page, and move on to tomorrow and show up ready to do the same thing.”
So, what could the Phillies and Braves possibly have in store for their winner-take-all showdown?
While that’s the biggest question looming over the National League Wild Card Series, it’s far from the only one. Here’s everything you need to know about Game 3:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
The game will begin at 8 p.m. ET and air on NBC and Peacock.
The Wild Card Series will be available in Spanish on Universo, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games, beginning with the Wild Card Series.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Phillies: TBD
The Phillies planned to meet following Game 2 to discuss their pitching plans for this week’s third elimination game. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said Monday that Aaron Nola was setting up to start Game 3, but there’s no question things can change. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see ace Zack Wheeler start on short rest. If he doesn’t start, there’s no doubt he’d enter the game in relief.
Braves: TBD
Grant Holmes will attempt to handle the bulk of the innings. But the Braves haven’t said whether he’ll start or possibly follow an opener. The top options to open are left-handers Ray Kerr or Brent Suter. Either would be tasked with handling Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber in the first inning.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Braves: The Braves’ lineup appears much more formidable against right-handed pitchers. With Mike Yastrzemski in left field, Mauricio Dubón would move to shortstop, which was where Ha-Seong Kim started during the first two games.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Phillies: Mattingly said it’s “all hands on deck,” although closer Jhoan Duran wasn’t available in Game 2. Mattingly said he hoped he’d have Duran in Game 3. But other than Cristopher Sánchez, who started Game 2, probably every pitcher on the Phillies’ staff will be available in some capacity in Game 3. That’s everybody from Wheeler to Luzardo to Painter.
Braves: Closer Raisel Iglesias and his top setup men Didier Fuentes and Dylan Lee both pitched in the first two games of this series. Each should be available in this winner-take-all game. Robert Suarez hasn’t been utilized yet. He missed three months with an elbow ailment before making two appearances last week. But manager Walt Weiss may have no other choice but to turn to the right-hander, who posted a 0.56 ERA in 31 appearances before his elbow became a problem in June.
Any injuries of note?
Braves: OF Lane Thomas could be available during the NLDS. Starting pitchers Bryce Elder (arthroscopic knee surgery), Reynaldo López (right shoulder inflammation) and Martín Pérez (lower back discomfort) may also be available in future rounds.
Who is hot and who is not?
Phillies: Home runs often come in bunches for Schwarber and Harper. Did their back-to-back homers in the eighth inning in Game 2 get them going? Bohm is 3-for-8 with one double and one home run in the series. After struggling all season, Realmuto has two hits and two RBIs this series.
Anything else fans might want to know?
The Phillies are 1-3 in franchise history in win-or-go-home postseason games. They won Game 5 of the 1980 NLCS. They lost Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS, Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS and Game 5 of the 1981 NLDS.

HOUSTON -- There was a moment with nobody out in the sixth inning Wednesday night during Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series that perfectly encapsulated the White Sox remarkable season and the downright fun they’ve had along the way.
Chase Meidroth connected on a three-run home run off Bryan Abreu, turning a one-run lead into a 7-3 advantage, which was ultimately the final score. But it was Meidroth’s reaction that reinforced the point.
Meidroth pumped his fist and screamed with joy from the moment he connected until he touched home plate, his emotions on full display. Back in the visitors’ clubhouse, the champagne was chilling as the White Sox prepared to take another somewhat unexpected step in the postseason.
“When I’m locked in on the field, I don’t know what goes through my mind,” Meidroth said. “All I’m thinking about is me and the baseball and trying to compete. But I had a good feeling.”
Good feelings have surrounded the White Sox since Spring Training, even dating back to SoxFest in late January. They’ve arguably been baseball’s best story in 2026, and perhaps one of the best in sports.
But this two-game sweep against the undermanned Astros proved they are a talented team to be reckoned with throughout the postseason. They are more than the young, energetic squad that shook off three consecutive 100-plus-loss campaigns to reach the playoffs.
Their second clubhouse celebration in a week -- and one of five they hope to have this postseason -- marked their first playoff series victory since 2005. That last series victory was a four-game sweep over the Astros in the World Series, with Games 3 and 4 played at what is now Daikin Park.
“These players are scared of nothing,” White Sox general manager Chris Getz said. “And whether it be myself or others, it’s like, 'How do we continue to nurture and fuel this group?'”
"We were able to do that with two games that I thought were emblematic of how we've won all season,” manager Will Venable said. “Contributions from everywhere. Sammy [Antonacci] setting the tone, great job down the lineup with everyone behind him. Guys pitching in different spots, going out whenever and getting the job done, and they did it."
For the second straight game, Chicago took control in the first inning with the help of Houston's poor defense. The White Sox scored four runs off Astros ace Hunter Brown, who had a 6-0 record with a 2.39 ERA over six career starts against the White Sox entering Wednesday.
Antonacci doubled on a line drive to left field that Yordan Alvarez seemed to have a play on but didn’t make. Kyle Teel singled home Antonacci, and Miguel Vargas reached on third baseman Nick Allen’s fielding error.
Andrew Benintendi singled home a second run, and when Lucas Spence's throw home got away from catcher Yainer Diaz, Vargas scored the third run. Tristan Peters then added an RBI single to cap the scoring in the opening frame.
Houston crept back with solo home runs from Jeremy Peña, Cam Smith and Jose Altuve off White Sox ace Sean Burke, who struck out eight over four innings. The Astros had a golden opportunity in the fifth inning, putting runners on first and second with one out for Alvarez. Anthony Kay was on the mound for his first true relief appearance this season.
Kay fell behind in the count, 3-0, threw a pitch in the zone that was taken by Alvarez and then got him to fly out to Antonacci in left on the next pitch. Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases, but Altuve flied out to right to end the frame.
Then Meidroth provided breathing room in the sixth, launching his three-run homer to restore Chicago’s four-run lead. Twelve outs stood between the White Sox and playoff history, but they had reasserted control, and Erick Fedde handled the final two innings to finish it off.
“You saw how it was this series,” Kay said. “Everyone didn't worry about themselves, just played as a team and did the best they could.”
“Hard to imagine myself in that situation, honestly, but I'm so glad they chose me with the ball and to give the team the win,” Fedde said. “This whole fan base deserved [this]. This whole organization deserved [this]. Feels good to move on to the next round.”
And now, it’s on to Cleveland and the AL Division Series for the White Sox, in the ongoing saga between AL Central rivals. The White Sox won the season series, 7-6, but the Guardians won the division by one game to earn home-field advantage.
Cleveland features a strong rotation and one of the best closers in the game in Cade Smith. Then again, the Guardians will see a team on a roll that has been 21 years in the making.

ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength.
“I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. Every once in a while, they get you.”
Nearly 40 years later, Weiss still remembers the sting he and his A’s teammates felt when an injured Gibson came off the bench to hit a walk-off homer against Hall of Fame closer Dennis Eckersley in Game 1 of the 1988 World Series at Dodger Stadium.
A similar type of sting was felt as the Braves blew a two-run eighth-inning lead in a 4-3, 10-inning loss to the Phillies in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Dylan Lee surrendered consecutive homers to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper in the eighth. Didier Fuentes allowed Alec Bohm’s decisive homer with two outs in the 10th.
“That's life,” Braves starting pitcher Tyler Mahle said. “Sometimes, it happens. There's nothing really else to say about it. It sucks now, but we're going to have a chance to go out there tomorrow and turn it around.”
Now, Weiss’ bunch must win Game 3 on Thursday to avoid being eliminated from the playoffs by Philadelphia for the fourth time overall and third time in the past five years. The Phillies eliminated Atlanta teams that won 100-plus regular-season games in 1993 (NLCS), 2022 (NLDS) and 2023 (NLDS).
Thursday's Game 3, airing on NBC and Peacock, will start at 8 p.m. ET.
“[The Braves] have played great at home,” Harper said. “But again, I'll just talk about the postseason; it's just a different animal.”
Mahle proved he was up to the challenge during what was his first postseason appearance. The right-hander, acquired from the Giants on Aug. 2, became the first Braves pitcher to allow one run or none over seven-plus innings in the postseason since Max Fried threw seven scoreless against the Reds in Game 1 of the 2020 NL Wild Card Series.
Once Harper misplayed a Drake Baldwin fly ball into a go-ahead double off Phillies starter Cristopher Sánchez during Atlanta’s two-run seventh, it looked like the Braves were destined for a great storyline.
But instead of celebrating how their trade acquisition helped them end the Phillies’ playoff dominance, the Braves were reminded that Lee hasn’t been nearly as good as he was before the All-Star break, when he posted a 1.47 ERA in 43 innings (44 appearances).
When Schwarber opened the eighth with a Statcast-projected 447-foot homer and Harper followed by depositing another ball into the right-field seats, Lee extended the troubles he had while posting a 6.00 ERA in 24 innings after the break. It should be noted he allowed just two homers during that stretch, and he did not allow any home runs to left-handed batters during the regular season.
“Lee’s our high-leverage lefty,” Weiss said. “He put down the same part of the order yesterday.”
Lee struck out Schwarber and got Harper to fly out in Game 1. How might he fare if he’s asked to go through these left-handed sluggers for a third straight day?
How about Fuentes? The rookie right-hander was masterful during the regular season, posting a 2.05 ERA in 70 1/3 innings as a reliever. But he surrendered J.T. Realmuto’s two-run triple in Game 1, and his psyche was bruised again Wednesday when Bohm sneaked his game-winning homer over the right-field wall.
“[Fuentes] made a good pitch,” Baldwin said. “I think if we need him tomorrow, he'll be ready to go, and I don't think he'll let that affect him too much.”
The Phillies’ rotation was a concern entering this series because Zack Wheeler was needed to pitch on Sunday with a postseason spot on the line. Well, Aaron Nola and Wheeler could be used in Game 3.
As for the Braves, they haven’t announced who will start Game 3. Grant Holmes will be lined up to pitch at least four innings. But will he start? Or will either Ray Kerr or Brent Suter take the mound as an opener?
More importantly, can the Braves bounce back from this and finally end their playoff struggles against their division rivals?

Dansby Swanson addressed the media at Petco Park ahead of Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series to discuss the Chicago Cubs' mindset following a Game 1 loss.
Watch the video below:
Q. You guys have talked all season long about this team's ability to kind of reset and start anew each new day. Are you seeing that so far today, and how do you think that's going to be able to benefit you guys today?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think we've all -- this whole year we've had opportunities to respond to adversity, and this is obviously no different. We have such a professional group, a group that prides itself on getting better each and every day no matter the circumstance. So business as usual in that regard.
Q. What is it like knowing you guys have Gausman starting tonight, given his experience in big playoff moments like this and just seeing his track record?
DANSBY SWANSON: He's pitched in a lot of big games in his career, in his life. We were thrilled to be able to acquire him at the deadline just knowing that experience and what he brings, the toughness, the pitch ability, and being able to have him on our team to help navigate through moments like this is a big part of why he's here.
He's been so good for us all year in big moments, and I expect nothing different tonight.
Q. From your experience, what's the key in games like today?
DANSBY SWANSON: Really and truly, it's just about being locked in on every pitch, just laying it all out there and understanding that we're at our best when we do what we do best.
At this time of year, it can be challenging because you go so in depth with the other team and trying to navigate what they're going to do, what we're going to do. I think the greatest reminder is, if we do what we do best, then we feel like we're a really good baseball team.
Q. Yesterday Craig went with Pedro at third. Today he goes with Matt Shaw. You saw what Pedro did when you were out. Just what's it like knowing those are the two guys you have behind the main group when something happens with Bregman or happened with you or somebody else?
DANSBY SWANSON: The depth of this group has definitely been a strength, a guy who's able to play multiple positions, able to put together great at-bats off different types of pitchers, and really just the personality piece. Great guys in the clubhouse and the ability to just add to our roster in terms of whether it's hitting left-handed pitching, right-handed pitching, being able to play second base, third base, slide around wherever is needed.
Without them, I doubt that we're in a position that we're in right now. So thankful for those guys, thankful for what they bring every day. Very glad that they're on our team.
Q. We've asked Bregman questions like every day since that day in Cincinnati, and he came back so quickly. Can you just put it into context, like what he's done and kind of what he's playing through and how kind of crazy it is when you take a step back and see what's happened over the past ten days or so?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think, if anyone knows Breggy, some facial fractures weren't going to stop him. He's dedicated to this game. He's dedicated to his craft. He's dedicated to his teammates, trying to find ways each and every day to not only personally get better, but to be able to help guys on the team get better.
It's been so fun being able to be on a team with him, just seeing what he does every day and what he brings to a group. I expect nothing else out of him at this point, doing whatever he can to be able to go out there, take the field. He knows that we're better when he's out there.
Q. Obviously you didn't really get much game action coming back from your injury. Just how have you been feeling with where your swing is at and just your comfort level in the box?
DANSBY SWANSON: Obviously baseball is a game that's meant to be played every day. When you miss a significant amount of time, it presents its own challenges coming back into it. I think kind of somewhat accepting that and going through the rehab process and understanding the position I was going to need to be in in order to get back to be as good as I can be was something that did drive me during that timeout.
It's like unfortunately, but also fortunately, having that time to be able to just kind of reflect and be able to do whatever I can to get back on the field and help this team win baseball games.
That's what I feel is a strength of mine as part of this group, and so thankful to be part of a group that is willing to step up in each and every way and not to overly say that I have to be the one to get things done or whatever. We're a group, we're a team, and we continue to push forward in that way.
Q. What's it been like to see Pete do what he's done this year with the idea that he's still so early in his career and he's got so much more to learn from and use to get better over the years?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think one of the really impressive things about Pete is the thing we've always seen, the physical ability, just the tools that he has, the strength, the defense, the base running. But to be able to really slow the game down this year and understand what he's trying to do at the plate to be able to -- I don't know if we've seen as significant of like a change in like walk rate or swing rate and all those kinds of things as we have with him.
He's just gotten so good at knowing what he's trying to do, how he's trying to execute, and been really stubborn at sticking to that. I think that's one of the big reasons why you've seen his game go into a new level is the ability to like mentally process things much quicker than it was earlier in his career. I think obviously that will only continue to get better.
To be able to do that at such a young age with more or less the different pressures you may have on you and attention on you, he's handled it so gracefully. It's been really, really cool to watch. Obviously having been somewhat in his shoes before and then being on like the older side, the veteran side of things, it's really cool to see him go through that and handle things the way he does.
Q. Obviously you guys have one of the best defenses in baseball, MVP candidate having a crazy, great season, and one of the best offenses. How important is it to take advantage of a season like this when you have the opportunity in the playoffs?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think each year is its own year, right? I think we don't really pay too much attention to those kinds of things. I think this group knows what it's capable of, so it's always reaching for the highest of heights that it can. That's one thing that I do love about this group is the relentless pursuit of really greatness together.
That's something that we've done all year. It's been kind of like a consistent mentality of ours all year. That's why it's so fun to be in positions like this because this is -- you know, being in situations like this is something that can only add to that confidence and to that mentality.
Q. Maybe a dumb question, but you guys from a distance obviously have a phenomenal defense. You've got great defensive players. That's got to be a huge part of it. Do you feel like this team maybe the last couple years compared to other teams you've been on puts an extra emphasis on that at all or goes out of the way to take advantage of the fact that you have the kind of defensive talent you do?
DANSBY SWANSON: It's almost like the last of a dying breed, right? Just like defense, no matter how great we've been offensively and the things we've done on the base pass, defense really is kind of our calling card.
It's interesting because it's not like something I would say that we like go above and beyond to work on it more. Jed and company have put together a great defensive roster obviously because we understand that defense really can change games. When you have Gold Glove-caliber defenders all over the yard, it makes it really tough on teams.
We understand that going out there and doing our part makes it hard for people to score on us. It's really fun to be a part of something like that. Give a lot of credit to the front office for being able to put together a team that is capable of doing more things than just playing defense, but it's wild when you go from really great defenses to not great defenses and like how much it can change things. We've been so consistent at remaining true to ourselves all year.
Q. Yesterday Gausman was saying that you treat this game like any other game except there's all those yellow towels flying around, and it can feel like momentum in these games in the postseason can feel even more real. What's it like managing that side of the game and the postseason?
DANSBY SWANSON: The biggest thing is accepting that it is the same game, right? It's the same rules other than the extra innings if there's not somebody on second base. But it's the same rules.
And being able to embrace that we are prepared and we've just got to go leave it all out there each and every day, each and every pitch, every inning and understanding that things can turn it one swing of the bat, one play in the field, one pitch, and just consistently attacking each and every pitch, whether it's on offense or defense.
Q. The pitching staff has obviously been through a lot this season. Can you just describe what it's been like watching how Counsell, the staff have pieced it together, especially at this point in the season and in a game like this where obviously it's all hands on deck?
DANSBY SWANSON: It's kind of wild when you like kind of ride it out, just the injuries that we've sustained, the things that we've gone through in the pitching department itself. Give a lot of credit to the guys that are here now, obviously Tommy and the rest of the pitching staff for being able to consistently find ways to improve the group and get guys better.
Then you look at just some of the acquisitions and all those kinds of things and really being able to identify traits that are going to play well at this time of year. It's really impressive what Counsell is able to do really putting each guy in a great position to succeed. It sounds simple, but he does it at a really, really high rate. I think it's something that he's really, really good at.
He's done well for the pitching staff, and they've obviously rewarded him in the same way by throwing the ball well. Very thankful for that and the hard work that everyone's done to be able to get to this point. Hopefully we'll go out there and put together a complete performance tonight.
